From the late 1980s onward, industry-standard, widely recognized benchmarks such as SPEC CPU (founded 1988), TPC-A/C/H/DS, SAP SD, and later MLPerf became the dominant way vendors and buyers compared system performance, emphasizing repeatability, clear metrics, and published methodologies. These benchmarks explicitly formalized dimensions like throughput and price/performance, and in some cases availability and recovery characteristics, aligning closely with the claim that valid measures come from standardized, easily duplicated tests. However, by the 2000s–2020s it was also widely acknowledged that such benchmarks can be gamed and often fail to represent real-world workloads, so practitioners increasingly supplemented them with bespoke workload testing rather than treating them as the single “best” way to assess performance.

The use of a 95th-percentile 1-second response-time requirement directly anticipates how OLTP benchmarks (e.g., TPC-C in the 1990s) and later web/SaaS SLAs and SRE practice came to standardize on percentile-based latency objectives rather than simple averages. Likewise, normalizing a five-year hardware/software/maintenance TCO by sustained transaction rate foreshadows the cost-per-transaction and cost-per-tpmC metrics in TPC benchmarks, and later cloud-era economics where services like AWS, Azure, and GCP are routinely evaluated on total cost per request/transaction over multi‑year horizons. Both aspects of the methodology align closely with how performance and economics of transactional systems were benchmarked and purchased from the 1990s through the 2020s.
